earlier_scan.source_named: Glottolog med: all four sources (Kennedy 1935, Devung 1981, Guerreiro 1996, Smith 2017) are wordlist-or-less; no grammar/phonology of Bahau exists.

sources.citation: Blust, Robert A. 1977. Sketches of the Morphology and Phonology of Bornean Languages 1: Uma Juman (Kayan). Papers in Western Austronesian Linguistics No. 2, Pacific Linguistics A-33: 7-122. DOI 10.15144/PL-A33.8
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request); access check: online with a university library login
sources.note: NOT Bahau (Uma Juman = Balui/Rejang Kayan [ree], Sarawak). p. 76 rule 8 (stress placement): 'In citation forms the last vowel of a word receives stress. Stress is penultimate within the phrase.' Recorded only as the nearest published Kayan statement; not transferable to Bahau.

sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing on stress; Crossref hits for 'Bahau' are all ethnography/folklore (hudoq ritual, Dayak Bahau music); no linguistic description of Bahau surfaced.

sources.note: 19,000 speakers (2007 SIL), Kutai Barat regency, classification Kayanic > Kayan Proper; no typology line, nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Smith, Alexander D. 2018. Kayanic comparative vocabularies (ADS2-001, readme + csv, 1178 rows, 14 lects incl. Bahau Saq). Kaipuleohone, University of Hawai'i. http://hdl.handle.net/10125/81770
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Phonetic IPA wordlist; 677 Bahau Saq entries, 328 carry a vowel-length mark on the final syllable (e.g. tutuːŋ, bateːʔ, afoːʔ), none carries a stress mark; readme has no prose on stress.

sources.citation: Smith, Alexander D. 2017. The Languages of Borneo: A Comprehensive Classification. PhD dissertation, University of Hawai'i at Manoa. 724 pp.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request); access check: not located online or in the libraries checked
sources.note: Bahau ('Bahau Saq', Tring on the middle Mahakam; consultants Pak Hibau and Simon Devung, language list p. 11, Fig. 9 p. 51) appears only in comparative sound-correspondence tables of ch. 2.2.1 Kayan (pp. 51-62); no stress statement for Bahau or Kayan proper. Stress is stated only for other Kayanic lects: Murik 'weak penultimate stress' (p. 63), Merap 'strong word-final stress' (p. 62) / 'a stress-final language, where the final syllable is always stressed' (p. 68), Segai-Modang 'strong word-final stress, an areal feature' (p. 73).

sources.citation: Blust, Robert. 2002. Formalism or phoneyism? The history of Kayan final glottal stop. In Adelaar & Blust (eds.), Between worlds: linguistic papers in memory of David John Prentice, Pacific Linguistics 529: 29-37.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Kayan dialects incl. Busang; nothing on stress, Bahau not mentioned.

sources.citation: Guerreiro, Antonio J. 1996. Homophony, sound changes and dialectal variations in some central Bornean languages. Mon-Khmer Studies 25: 205-226.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Ethnolinguistic overview of Kayanic incl. the 'Bahau' isolects (Bahau Sa', Bahau Hwang Triing) with lexical comparisons; no mention of stress or accent anywhere. Reference list (pp. 216-218) shows the only Bahau-specific items are Devung 1981a/b (passive, pronouns) and Devung 1984 Swadesh word-list of Bahau Triing (ms.).
